speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Further to the Minister for Health's Statement, I will now elaborate on the approach my Ministry has adopted to continue the safe and orderly restoration of Singapore's air connectivity.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: My Statement will also address Oral Question No 4 by Mr Melvin Yong in today's Order Paper.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Throughout this process, our top priority has been protecting the health of our aviation workers, travellers and the broader community.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: We work closely with MOH to monitor the evolving global COVID-19 situation and implement enhanced measures as necessary.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: For example, with the recent rise in cases globally, we have stepped up our Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) requirements for all airport workers performing passenger-facing and janitorial duties.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The Changi aviation community stakeholders are also making a concerted effort to push and ensure that airport workers are well protected by keeping their vaccination up to date.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Apart from vaccination centres islandwide, they can now also get their booster shots at the newly established facility at the Raffles Medical Group clinic at Terminal 3.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Our aviation community will stay vigilant and stands ready to respond quickly should there be a material change in MOH's risk assessment, such as the emergence of a new Variant of Concern (VOC).

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: This is the new normal for aviation as we emerge from COVID-19.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: This has given our aviation stakeholders valuable lead time to build up their capacity, while recruiting and training their workforce.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: As China reopens its borders, we will continue with this cautious approach to ensure that Changi Airport has the capacity to manage the ramp-up in flights, provide clarity and certainty to airlines, and ensure that passengers have a safe and smooth experience.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The number of weekly flights at Changi Airport has also recovered to nearly 80% of pre-COVID-19 levels.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: As at end October 2022, we had 25 weekly flights between China and Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: As both sides gradually increased flight connectivity, this rose to 36 weekly flights around mid-December 2022.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: This works out to an average of five to six flights per day at Changi.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: To put this in context, it is less than 10% of the number of flights pre-COVID-19 between China and Singapore – about 400 – and about 1.5% of the total flights handled by Changi today.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: We receive about 700 to 1,000 inbound passengers from China daily, which again is about 1% to 1.5% of the total daily arrivals at Changi.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: This is also less than 10% of pre-COVID-19 levels.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: We welcome China's recent moves to restore quarantine-free travel with the rest of the world.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Singapore enjoys longstanding and multifaceted relations with China.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: It is in the interest of both our countries to restore our air connectivity in a safe and orderly manner.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: After China's recent announcement that it will reopen its borders and remove quarantine requirements for returning travellers with effect from yesterday, Singapore and Chinese airlines have applied to operate more flights between the two countries.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: CAAS is evaluating and will progressively approve these applications.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: As with other countries previously, we will carefully restore air connectivity with China, taking into consideration the prevailing public health assessment as well as Changi's capacity, so that we can ensure efficient operations and a safe and smooth travel experience.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: In summary, Mr Speaker, we will continue to adhere to our careful and calibrated approach in the restoration of air connectivity with China.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: This measured approach has enabled a safe and orderly resumption of Singapore's air connectivity with the world, while we monitor the outcomes and evolving public health situation, assess the operational impact and decide on further moves.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: It has allowed Changi to manage the recovery relatively well, while making it possible for Singaporeans and residents to travel again for work, leisure and to see loved ones.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: It has also spurred the economic recovery of our tourism-related sectors, as well as consumer-facing industries and the professional services.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The aviation community in Changi remains vigilant and is prepared to respond quickly if there are material changes in the operating environment.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: At all times, our priority is to protect the health of our aviation workers, travellers and the broader community.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: First, as the bivalent vaccine booster shot is currently optional, I would like to ask the Minister whether the take-up rate among our elderly and the at-risk groups is adequate.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The second question – given that there have been news reports on the increased transmissibility and re-infection rates of some of the virus' sub-variants circulating now, are more extensive communication efforts being planned to encourage more people to take their bivalent boosters as soon as possible?

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We have never made it compulsory, but because of the cooperation and social consciousness of Singaporeans, we have attained a very high vaccination rate.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Today, instead of measuring bivalent take-up rate, let us measure the up-to-date vaccination rate.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But I think the Member raises an important question – how do we ensure that people continue to take it?

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We will continue to use the measures that have worked.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We now have Joint Testing and Vaccination Centres (JTVCs) throughout the island.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: You do not have to make an appointment.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Thirdly – and I think that is MOH's job, the Multi-Ministry Task Force (MTF)'s job – continue to publicly explain the benefits of vaccination, because the benefits far outweigh the risks of getting COVID-19 and the risk of having severe illnesses.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: If more people take the vaccinations, when they meet each other for coffee, they find that their friends have taken them, they feel the fear of missing out (FOMO), and then, they will take too.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I have two questions for the Minister for Transport.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: First, given the heightened risk profile of international travellers, would Singapore consider temporarily tightening the mask-wearing policy to require masks to be worn on board all flights entering Singapore, so that we can reduce the risk of in-flight COVID-19 contamination?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I think we all believe that masks act as the first line of defence against the spread of the virus.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Second, as Minister Ong mentioned earlier, COVID-19 wastewater surveillance has shown to be a valuable tool.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Airplane wastewater surveillance could potentially be an option.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Would Singapore consider stepping up sampling wastewater taken from international aircraft entering Singapore to track any emerging new variants?

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: I would leave the wastewater question to the Minister for Health, who can speak on it more authoritatively.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: On the point on mask-wearing, today, specifically with respect to China, the airlines already require mask-wearing for their crew as a precautionary measure.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Also, China already requires mask-wearing for flights going in and coming out.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, in a sense, that has already been addressed.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Our general posture on mask-wearing is really for compliance with the source country's or destination country's requirements.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: If you are going to a country that requires the wearing of masks whilst in flight, then the airline will advise you to do so, and then, you wear the mask; and likewise, on the return leg.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: In general, we have aligned our mask-wearing protocols with the protocols that we have worked out with MOH for the domestic setting.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: That continues to be the way we will operate unless there are material reasons for us to make a deviation or an exception.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Minister Iswaran left the wastewater testing to me.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: As I mentioned in my Statement, wastewater testing, at least for the ones we use in Singapore, works by detecting viral fragments from solid waste, not from urine.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Therefore, we used it in dormitories, in housing estates, even in nursing homes, which is quite a challenge because many old folks use diapers.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Therefore, for a flight from China to Singapore, it is quite a short duration.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, I think that the use of wastewater test will capture a very small sample and is, therefore, not very useful.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: I have a supplementary question for Minister Ong.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: Minister Ong said we required the tourists, the in-flights, people – if they did board the plane, they have to declare their vaccination status right now.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: What is the definition of a full vaccination for that matter, because in Singapore, the full vaccination status, it is three shots if you take non-mRNA.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We do require medical insurance if you are not fully vaccinated.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, our definition is quite a tight one.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The World Health Organization (WHO) has a more relaxed definition.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We know our definition is different and stricter than WHO's, which is currently applied on travellers.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Having said that, the current definitions have worked well for us so far.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But we will have to study if there is a need to review the definitions for vaccination status based on the development of the disease threat.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I want to thank Minister for Health and the Minister for Transport for the very useful Statements that help to prepare Singaporeans as China opens up, to lead as normal a life as possible as we have been very steadfast, as we had our opening measures.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I wanted to seek a clarification from Minister Ong.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Should a new and dangerous variant emerged, what is likely the protocol that will be adopted, as most Singaporeans have cooperated and been fully vaccinated, and also gotten used to the concept of living with COVID-19 as an endemic as a way of life?

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: A clarification for Minister Iswaran: what is MOT's projected timeline for travellers from China to return to pre-COVID-19 volume?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: What do we do when we detect a new dangerous variant?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, if you jump at every one, you will be jumping every day, twice, right?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Because sub-variants can really differ very minimally; just like a human, you are wearing a different shirt, different watch, different shoes, different earrings.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, we cannot jump at every sub-variant, no matter how sexy the name sounds.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But keep our eyes and ears on the ground with the global surveillance system.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Look out for those that is more dangerous.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: If there is one, then we think about what we should do.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And we can see how some countries are implementing.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Mr Melvin Yong suggested masks on planes – which is not unthinkable – pre-departure test (PDT) and so on and so forth.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Therefore, if you want PDT to be a little more tight, you also implement an OAT, on-arrival test.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But still, for a short flight, you might be incubating before you board and also during landing.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And then, for the next three days you are incubating.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And therefore, that is still not enough, you want to be even tighter, you implement SHN, stay-home notice.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: That was what we did – PDT, OAT, SHN.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And soon, you have a big border control system, testing everyone before they board; testing everyone after they board, dedicated a taxi driving you to your homes and then using devices to make sure they stay at home.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And then, that is still not foolproof, because one day, a traveller may pass it to a driver, and the driver goes home, he goes for big lo-hei dinner, passes it to many other people.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And then, next thing you need to think about is safe management measures (SMMs), social restrictions.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We always have the mindset that border measures are a substitute for domestic community measures.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Once you implement one, you must be prepared that the rest are going to follow because that is how transmissible the virus is.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: One is not the substitute of the other.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We know it will not shut out the virus, but it buys us time for scientific data to come out, because in a matter of weeks, you can know the characteristics and the parameters that matter.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: To what extent does it translate into severe cases?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Does it affect old people more or young people more?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Once you know these parameters, then you can decide your next step.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: If the parameters turned out that it is not something very serious, then you can stand down, false alarm.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: There will be some damage to livelihoods and inconveniences but, at least, we stand down.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But if your nightmare comes true, that it is very transmissible and very deadly, then, you have to hunker down.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We have to hunker down again, back to almost square one – contact tracing, SMMs, border measures, everything come in, again, to buy us even more time.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Even more time so that a new effective vaccine can come on stream.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The Member asked about protocol to respond to a new dangerous variant.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But when something like that happens, expect lots of uncertainties, some confusion.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It would not be straightforward, a lot of judgement calls will be required.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Having said that, I am reluctant to put a timeline to this process and the reason is because there are several variables that we need to take into account.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: First, just from a commercial point of view, the number of applications from airlines and so on, although all indications are that there will be strong demand.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: But, beyond that is, of course, the public health situation that is evolving.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Our desire is really to do this in a systematically calibrated manner because whilst the destination is important, the journey is even more so at this juncture.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: And honestly, sometimes knowing too much or too little makes people feel helpless over things they cannot control and trigger a lot of anxiety.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: I have seen a lot of anxious people in the past three years as a clinical doctor.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I cannot disagree with what the doctor just summarised.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: To see a summary of what I have just said, my speech will be on the MOH website.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: I am not sure if it is for the Minister for MOT or MOH.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: In the past before COVID-19, returning Singaporeans do not need to do health declaration at the customs.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: But now, we have to do it via online or physical.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: I mean, I can understand that we need to do some of these border checks, like PDTs, but for the SG Arrival Card where we ask some generic questions: where you come from, Africa or Latin America or Middle East.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: And then, ask those questions like, "in the last seven days, have you been unwell" and so on.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We can say yes to all three questions, but you will still be granted entry, you will still be allowed entry to Singapore and there is no follow-up.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: I just want to ask whether what purpose does this serve to do that, to have that SG Arrival Card process?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This is one of those things that MOH gets all the time.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: If you succumb and then you remove it, and then, one day you regret, that you should have kept it.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We have always had an SG Arrival Card and it is physical.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, now, the SG Arrival Card has become a digital declaration.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And in that process, MOH, with the Immigration and Checkpoints Authority (ICA) has very thoroughly gone through and reduced the questions to the bare minimum, to the extent that the Member feels it may not be so helpful.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It is one of those things we keep in the background – useful to have, and if we need to trigger some action, the information will be valuable.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I understand that currently, in terms of bed utilisation and the intensive care unit (ICU) utilisation, the capacity levels are very high – for some of the public hospitals is 90% or even, well above 90%.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: So, notwithstanding the regime of PDT and full vaccination, it will just take a relatively small number of cases coming in to possibly strain the hospital capacity to a very difficult position.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: So, I am just wondering if the Government has thought through this extreme or worst-case scenario that might happen with the opening up, of capacity being overstrained in a public hospital system.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The second question is on the prescription of Paxlovid, which is the COVID-19 anti-viral drug.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I understand that there are 36 clinics now that can prescribe it.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Is there plan to expand this across the whole primary healthcare system?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: On hospital capacity, indeed, this is one of the key considerations I mentioned in the Statement just now.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I cannot remember how many exactly, but it is in the low tens.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: COVID-19 affected that indirectly because it delayed the opening of some major public health facilities.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It will greatly relieve the burden currently of the high utilisation rate of hospital beds.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: That means for patients who do not require acute care, but waiting for step-down or rehabilitative care, they can go to a TCF first.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Manpower is another constraint, but we are recruiting, building up.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We lost a number of good nurses, especially foreign ones, because the competition heated up.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: These are some of the things we need to do, and you are right: we have to be very alert should there be a new variant or big influx of severe cases and implement the necessary measures.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: As for Paxlovid, we are constantly reviewing if more clinics can dispense them.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But so far, because of the fact that we are a very highly vaccinated population and Paxlovid is prescribed for people who are at-risk.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, actually the number of people who is need it, is not very high.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Notwithstanding, this is something we will look at.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The Minister mentioned just now about 38 weekly flights from China, while pre-COVID-19, there were 400.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, the Minister was trying to share the general trend that we would proceed through to pre-COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The Minister mentioned about the careful and calibrated approach.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: What does it mean, in terms of, it affecting our original plans?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For the whole of this year, we will eventually try to target future flights to be achieved by this year or potentially 2024.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: What does this careful and calibrated approach mean, in terms of changes to our original plans, to open up to reach pre-COVID-19 levels?

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Essentially, our starting point – and that has been the way since the latter half of last year – has really been to gear up our airport operational capacity to be able to manage volumes that are equal to pre-COVID-19 levels.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Indeed, that is where we are today – because Terminal 1, Terminal 3 and Terminal 4 are now fully operational.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And for Terminal 2, half of that is now able to take both arriving and departing flights.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: With that, and the improvements that have been made in the system and operationally, we are actually able to accommodate the volumes that were around – if I recall correctly – pre-COVID-19, which was about 68 million passengers a year.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, that is the supply side in terms of physical capacity.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: A second element is the manpower aspect, where we continue to recruit, to train, in order to build up the capability for the whole spectrum of services that are essential to run the airport well.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: In terms of manpower manning levels today, we are at about 90%, or slightly more.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: This continues to be an important effort but also a challenging one.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, this is an area which Changi Airport Group (CAG), Singapore Airport Terminal Services (SATS) and even Singapore Airlines (SIA) and others in the group, are working very hard at.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: But that could become one of the constraining factors.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Hence, the careful, calibrated approach, because we do not want to extend flight capacity without having the ken to deal with it at the airport side.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: This is the important dynamic that we are trying to balance.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Overall, as I replied to the earlier question, specifically with respect to China, we would like to restore air connectivity to pre-COVID-19 levels.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: There is a significant gulf as we are all well aware now from the data.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The real challenge is to do this in a safe and orderly manner.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: This is where I think both countries are aligned and we are seeking to do this in a systematic way.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: I cannot give a specific time frame but what I can say is, in the near term, we will continue to do this methodically.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: I do not expect it to be a surge, but neither are we going to be static or at a standstill.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Introduction of Government Bill, Minister for Sustainability and the Environment.
